title: Buttered Margins
passage:
The smell reaches the pavement before the poster does. Above the refreshment counter at the Lyric in Ardenshaw, two warm-air units push the scent of popping maize out through the foyer doors into the street, and the chain that fitted them makes no secret of why. Halvard Meng, who spent eleven years pricing screens for a mid-sized exhibitor before turning consultant, thinks the arrangement is the most honest thing about his trade. Of every pound taken at the box office in a film's opening week, he reckons, rather more than half goes back to the distributor; and a screen is an expensive box to keep warm, so what stays behind rarely covers the ___(1)___.

___(2)___, the counter is where the margin lives. Figures Meng gathered from four independent sites in 2024 put the gross margin on a tub of popcorn between eighty and ninety per cent: maize is cheap, oil is cheap, and the staff are standing there anyway. A ticket, by contrast, is a surprisingly ___(3)___ item on an exhibitor's accounts once the distributor has been paid, however dear it looks at the till.

The obvious objection is that audiences would rather pay less in the foyer, and one independent in the north set out to oblige them, halving every counter price for a season in 2023. Admissions rose by a little over four per cent. Takings, when the season's accounts were closed, had not risen with them but ___(4)___, and by the spring the old prices were quietly back. Meng reads the episode as a lesson about who is really being charged. The tub is not a levy added on top of a fair ticket; it is part of the fair price, collected from the third of the audience willing to pay it.

He is less comfortable about where that leaves things. The customers least able to walk past a counter are, as a rule, the ones with children in tow, and Meng has no ___(5)___ to offer them beyond the observation that the alternative is worse: take the foyer away, he argues, and the ticket does not fall but rises, and the family that came only for the film pays the difference. The smell in the street is not a trick played on an audience. It is a business paying for its roof.
— Ines Halloway, business columnist

questions.rationale: Collocation gap; all four are plural nouns built on the same over- prefix (POS-uniform, shape-matched). The frame — 'a screen is an expensive box to keep warm, so what stays behind rarely covers the ___' — needs the standing running costs of a building, and 'cover the overheads' is the locking English collocation. overtures = collocation_misfit (an opening move or a musical introduction; 'cover the overtures' is not English and names nothing a building costs). overhangs = collocation_misfit (a projecting part of a structure, or in finance an unsold surplus; one does not 'cover the overhangs' of a cinema). overspills = collocation_misfit (what spreads beyond a container or a city boundary; nothing here overflows). Only 'overheads' collocates with 'cover' and matches the heating-and-building cost the clause has just named.

Connective-logic gap; all four are sentence-initial -ly adverbs (connective class matched). The previous sentence establishes that ticket money 'rarely covers the overheads', and the gapped sentence states the result of that shortfall — 'the counter is where the margin lives' — which the following figures then confirm. The link is causal, so 'Consequently' is the only fit. Conversely = polarity_mirror/wrong_logic (demands an opposite, but the counter's margin follows from the box office's thinness rather than contradicting it). Ostensibly = wrong_logic (marks a claim as merely apparent and about to be undercut, whereas the paragraph immediately backs the claim with eighty-to-ninety-per-cent margins). Historically = wrong_logic (sets up a then-versus-now contrast the passage never supplies at this point; the 2024 figures are present-tense evidence, not a former state).

Sense-and-collocation gap; all four are un- + -able adjectives (POS-uniform, suffix-rhymed). The frame — 'A ticket, by contrast, is a surprisingly ___ item on an exhibitor's accounts once the distributor has been paid, however dear it looks at the till' — sets the ticket against a margin of 'between eighty and ninety per cent' and specifies the exhibitor's accounts after the distributor's share is gone, so the missing word must name poor return: 'unprofitable' locks. unaffordable = wrong-party misfit (it describes what a customer cannot pay for, not what an exhibitor earns; the clause is explicitly about the exhibitor's accounts, and 'however dear it looks at the till' has already conceded that the customer finds it expensive). unassailable = sense misfit (impossible to attack or dispute; an accounts item is not a position under challenge here). unrepeatable = sense misfit (not able to be done or said again, which contradicts a transaction the cinema makes at every screening). Only 'unprofitable' answers the contrast the frame builds.

Polarity gap with an alliterative past-tense set (POS-uniform, shape-matched). The frame 'had not risen with them but ___' is a not-X-but-Y construction that demands the opposite pole of 'risen', and the downstream evidence confirms it: 'by the spring the old prices were quietly back', which only makes sense if the discount cost the cinema money. 'slipped' supplies the required fall. soared = polarity_mirror (the reader who has just registered 'Admissions rose by a little over four per cent' reaches for a rising verb, but 'not risen ... but soared' contradicts itself and would leave the price reversal unexplained). swelled = polarity_mirror (same fault, and 'takings swelled' is the positive pole the frame has already excluded). sprouted = collocation_misfit with a thematic lure (the passage is full of maize, so a growing verb feels at home, but takings do not sprout in English). Only 'slipped' satisfies the inversion the frame demands.

Collocation gap; all four are singular rem- nouns (POS-uniform, shape-matched). The frame — 'Meng has no ___ to offer them beyond the observation that the alternative is worse' — concerns families who cannot avoid the counter, and the concessive 'beyond the observation that' signals that what he lacks is a cure for their problem: 'has no remedy to offer' is the locking collocation. reminder = sense misfit (a prompt to recall something; withholding a reminder would say nothing about the unfairness he has just conceded). remnant = sense misfit (a leftover scrap; nothing here remains over). remittance = collocation_misfit (a sum of money sent in payment; 'no remittance to offer them' would promise a refund the passage never raises, and the sentence goes on to offer an argument, not a payment). Only 'remedy' fits both the collocation and the concession the sentence is making.
